A few quick questions. Each one targets a line that anyone could have written, so your own answer can replace it. Skip any you like.

1. "Phone calls were hit or miss." In a sentence or two, the way you'd say it out loud: what did that look like at a clinic? For example, how many calls did the front desk make a day, or how often did anyone call back?
2. "Texts get read, and patients can confirm or reschedule in seconds." Do you have a number or a moment behind this, like a reply rate or how many patients now confirm by text? Or a case where a patient rescheduled by text and the slot got filled?
3. "The change was simple." What did you actually do? Which tool or service, what the message says, and how far ahead it goes out.
4. "Fewer empty chairs / Less time on the phone." Can you put a figure on either one, such as hours saved per clinic per week or appointments recovered?
5. "The lesson for me: sometimes the biggest operational wins come from meeting people where they already are." What did you think before this worked, or what surprised you? Say it the way you'd tell a colleague.

2. "Texts get read, and patients can confirm or reschedule in seconds." Do you have a number or a moment behind this, like a reply rate or how many patients now confirm by text? Or a case where a patient rescheduled by text and the slot got filled?
3. "The change was simple." What did you actually do? Which tool or service, what the message says, and how far ahead it goes out.

answers:
1. Honestly I don't have call numbers to give you, like calls per day or callback rates. What I can say is the old confirmation calls ate a lot of front desk time, about 11 hours a week now saved once we moved off them.

2. I don't have a reply rate or a specific rescheduling story I can point to. What I do know is that the real driver was two-way texting, where patients can reschedule just by replying, more than the reminders themselves.

3. We moved to a two-way text system across all 9 clinics, and it costs about $1,400 a month total. I can't name the vendor because the contract needs approval for that, and I don't have the message wording or how far ahead it goes out, so I'd skip that part.

4. Yes on hours: front desk staff save about 11 hours a week on confirmation calls, and I honestly think that's the bigger win. I don't have a per-clinic breakdown or a count of appointments recovered.

5. What I'd say is that it wasn't just "send reminders." The two-way part, letting people reschedule by replying, is what made the difference, and it isn't a magic fix. Joanna at our Gdańsk clinic noticed elderly patients would reply "OK" and still not show, so we now also phone everyone over 70. Sopot only got to 12% and nobody's sure why. I also worry a bit that our six months included summer, when no-shows tend to drop anyway.
reply2:
I built this from your answers and kept your wording where I could. I left out the vendor name, the message wording, and the send timing, since you don't have them or can't share them. A reply rate or a patient story would help the two-way texting claim land.

<final>
We cut no-shows at Brightwell Dental Group from 18% to 7% in six months, after moving all 9 of our clinics to a two-way text system. It costs about $1,400 a month for the whole group.

It wasn't just "send reminders." Patients can reschedule by replying to the text, and that two-way part is what made the difference.

The old confirmation calls ate a lot of front desk time. We now save about 11 hours a week, and I honestly think that's the bigger win. Every no-show is also a patient who didn't get treated and a slot someone else could have used.

It isn't a magic fix. Joanna at our Gdańsk clinic noticed that elderly patients would reply "OK" and still not show up, so we now also phone everyone over 70. Sopot only got to 12%, and nobody's sure why. I also worry a bit that our six months included summer, when no-shows tend to drop anyway, so the texting may not get all the credit.

If you run a multi-location practice and still rely on calls, it's worth testing.
</final>
